say.text: A 40% burn can need several litres of fluid in the first day. Why does so much volume leave the circulation?

choices.label: Capillary leak drains plasma out of the circulation for hours
The burn damages the heart, so it needs volume to restore output
The burn is infected, and sepsis needs large volume to clear it
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the burn does to the blood vessels first, before any infection or pump problem.
Right. Mediators from the burn and capillary leak pull plasma out of the circulation, so volume has to replace it.
That plasma loss makes burn shock hypovolaemic, and Ringer lactate is the fluid of choice.
That is not the right choice. A shocked burn patient can look like a failing pump, with a fast heart and low pressure, so the heart feels like the problem.
Myocardial depression is an added factor. The main problem is plasma loss, so the volume is for the circulation, not a failing pump.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the main cause first: plasma loss, with the heart as an added factor.

say.text: That is not the right choice. Fever and a sick look make sepsis feel like the cause, but sepsis tends to come later.
Early burn shock comes from the leak itself, so it is hypovolaemic (K17, K19).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate early burn shock from later sepsis: the leak comes first.

say.text: A 70 kg adult has a 40% scald, and you have confirmed the burn size. Now Parkland turns that into a fluid plan.

Current Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) practice starts **Ringer lactate** at how many mL per kg per %TBSA (percent total body surface area burned) in 24 hours, before you titrate to urine output?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the word **current** in the stem. The exam key and current practice are not the same figure.
Right. Current ATLS-style practice starts at about 2 mL per kg per %TBSA in adults, then titrates to urine output.
The **4 mL** you may have learnt is the classic Parkland figure, and PYQs expect it.
That is not the right choice. 4 mL is the classic Parkland figure, so every exam key has drilled it and it feels like the only formula.
Current practice starts lower, at about 2 mL in adults, and titrates to urine output to avoid fluid creep. Read the qualifier in the stem.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix this one properly: 4 mL is the exam key and 2 mL is current practice. Keep both side by side.

say.text: That is not the right choice. 3 mL sits between the two numbers you have seen, so it looks like a safe compromise.
Adult figures are about 2 mL in current practice and 4 mL in the exam key. 3 mL is neither.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin the adult figures down: 2 mL for current practice, 4 mL for the exam key.

say.text: Half of the total goes in the first 8 hours, and those 8 hours are counted from the **time of burn**.
Why does the clock start at the burn, and not when the patient reaches you?

choices.label: The leak starts at injury, so the deficit builds from the burn
The team takes over, so the clock starts when they do
Leak is worst in the first 8 hours, whenever it starts
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what makes fluid leave the circulation, and when that began.
Yes. The capillary leak starts at the injury and is heaviest in the first 8 to 12 hours, so the deficit is already building when you arrive.
So the window runs from the burn. A late arrival has lost hours that the clock has already counted.
Remember it as the burn clock, not the bed clock.
That is not the right choice. The team's arrival feels like a start, because that is when the chart and the drip begin.
The leak does not wait for the team. The first 8 hours run from the time of burn, not the time of arrival.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which clock the leak runs on: the injury's, not the team's.

say.text: That is not the right choice. The leak is heaviest early, so the first 8 hours feel like a window set by the hospital.
The window is fixed by when the leak began, which is the burn. Being heaviest early does not move the start.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie the window to the injury, not to how fast the leak runs.

say.text: Exam stem: a 70 kg adult with a 40% burn, the Parkland 4 mL formula, and you reach the patient at the time of burn.
What is the infusion rate for the first 8 hours?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Work in three steps: the 24-hour total, then the half that goes in the first 8 hours, then divide by the hours.
Right. The 24-hour total is 4 x 70 x 40 = 11,200 mL. Half, 5,600 mL, goes in the first 8 hours: 700 mL/h.
The other 5,600 mL runs over the next 16 hours, at 350 mL/h.
That is not the right choice. 1,400 mL/h looks like a rate, and it is the whole 24-hour volume squeezed into 8 hours.
Only half of 11,200 mL goes in the first 8 hours, so the rate is 700 mL/h.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the step: halve the total before you divide by the hours.

say.text: That is not the right choice. 350 mL/h is a real rate in this chain, which is why it tempts you when the halving is misplaced.
350 mL/h belongs to the next 16 hours. The first 8 hours get 5,600 mL at 700 mL/h.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the two windows apart: first 8 hours at 700 mL/h, next 16 hours at 350 mL/h.

say.text: Same patient: 70 kg, 40% burn, 4 mL formula, so 11,200 mL in 24 hours with half in the first 8 hours.
Which statement about this burn is **NOT** correct?

choices.label: Half, 5,600 mL, is run in the first 8 hours
The whole 11,200 mL is run in the first 8 hours
The next 16 hours run at 350 mL/h
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Work out what share of 11,200 mL the first 8 hours should get before you judge each statement.
Right. Running all 11,200 mL in 8 hours is the wrong model: the first 8 hours get half, 5,600 mL.
The other two statements are true, so the one that breaks the halving is the answer.
That is not the right choice: this statement is true, and the question asks for the false one. It tempts when the halving feels too small.
Half of 11,200 mL is 5,600 mL, and that is the first 8 hours' share.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check each statement against the 24-hour total before you judge it.

say.text: That is not the right choice: this statement is true, and the question asks for the false one. It tempts when the second half is confused with the first.
The next 16 hours get 5,600 mL, and 5,600 divided by 16 is 350 mL/h.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so label each window before you test its rate.

say.text: A 70 kg adult with a 40% burn reaches you 3 hours after the burn. The ambulance has already run 1,500 mL of Ringer lactate.
The first-half target is 5,600 mL. What do you prescribe?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask two questions: what has already gone in, and how much time is left before 8 hours from the burn?
Right. The 5,600 mL target minus the 1,500 mL already given leaves 4,100 mL, due by 8 hours from the burn, so 5 hours remain.
Titrate that hourly to urine output rather than running it as a fixed rate.
That is not the right choice. Leaving the ambulance fluid out of the sum feels tidy, since the target is the target.
Fluid given before arrival is deducted from the first-8-hour volume, so only 4,100 mL is still owed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so deduct first, then divide what remains by the hours left.

say.text: That is not the right choice. The deduction is right, so the answer looks almost complete.
But the 8 hours run from the time of burn, not from arrival, so only 5 hours are left.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count the 8 hours from the burn and subtract the hours already gone.

say.text: Fluid already given before arrival is deducted from the first-8-hour volume.
The drip is already running when you arrive. Why does it change what you prescribe?

choices.label: The formula replaces the drip, so the drip is stopped
It counts toward the first-half volume, so less remains
It is separate treatment, so the formula is added on top
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what the first-half volume is: a total the patient must reach, or a rate you start afresh.
Right. The first-half volume is a total the patient must receive by 8 hours from the burn, and the drip has already given part of it.
So you run only the remainder. Subtracting what has already gone in stops you giving the same fluid twice.
That is not the right choice. Treating the drip as separate sounds careful, since nothing already given seems to be touched.
The fluid already given counts toward the first-8-hour volume, so the total still owed shrinks.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count what has gone in against the target before you prescribe.

say.text: That is not the right choice. Stopping a running drip and restarting from zero looks like a clean reset.
The formula sets a target, and the volume already given counts toward it. Restarting from zero ignores what has gone in, so the patient gets more than the target.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the running volume in the sum rather than resetting it.
